# Context Engineering and Harness Engineering {#context-harness-engineering}

## Why these two terms matter

Earlier chapters covered prompting, verification loops, hooks, skills, and MCP
as separate techniques. Two newer terms give those techniques a common frame:

- **Context engineering** asks: *which tokens should the model see at this
  step?* It covers instructions, retrieved data, tool definitions, tool
  outputs, conversation history, and memory.
- **Harness engineering** asks: *what system around the model makes it reliable
  over many steps?* It covers the agent loop, tools, sandbox, state files,
  hooks, permissions, tests, and evaluation.

Both terms are young, and their boundaries are still debated. This chapter
separates three kinds of claim: concepts that are likely to last, vendor
practices and features that change quickly, and evidence. The evidence is
labeled by strength throughout.

**Source labels used in this chapter**

- **[Vendor]**: an organization reporting on its own product or results.
- **[Secondary]**: the original could not be read; the claim comes from a
  mirror, summary, or aggregator.
- **[Unverified]**: no primary source was found.

Product names, API identifiers, and preview status are as of October 2026.

Parts of this chapter began as study notes from the DeepLearning.AI course
*Context Engineering*, built with Chroma and taught by Chroma's CEO, Jeff
Huber. Its first module follows a customer-service agent, and its second a
coding agent investigating a customer-feedback app; this chapter borrows both
scenarios. Chroma sells retrieval infrastructure,
so its research claims carry the **[Vendor]** label like any other.

## Where the terms came from

### Context engineering (mid-2025)

The term spread through a cluster of posts in June and July 2025. No single
person has a verified claim to coining it, so "popularized by" is the accurate
phrasing.

- Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke described it as "the art of providing all the context
  for the task to be plausibly solvable by the LLM" (June 2025, quoted by
  [Simon Willison](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/27/context-engineering/)).
- Harrison Chase of LangChain defined it as building dynamic systems that give
  the model "the right information and tools in the right format," and credited
  earlier practitioners
  ([LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/blog/the-rise-of-context-engineering)).
- Andrej Karpathy called it "the delicate art and science of filling the context
  window with just the right information for the next step." He compared the
  model to a CPU and the context window to its RAM (June 2025, quoted by
  [Simon Willison](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/27/context-engineering/)).
- Drew Breunig named common ways long contexts fail
  ([How long contexts fail](https://www.dbreunig.com/2025/06/22/how-contexts-fail-and-how-to-fix-them.html);
  [How to fix your context](https://www.dbreunig.com/2025/06/26/how-to-fix-your-context.html)).
- Manus published lessons from running a production agent
  ([Manus, July 2025](https://manus.im/blog/Context-Engineering-for-AI-Agents-Lessons-from-Building-Manus)).
- Anthropic's engineering guide (29 September 2025) gave the most-cited
  definition: strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens
  during LLM inference
  ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)).
- The DeepLearning.AI and Chroma course uses a three-part working definition:
  giving the agent **the right information, in the right format, at the right
  time** for its current task. Section \@ref(right-info-format-time) uses it as
  a design checklist.

### Harness engineering (early 2026)

"Harness" and "scaffold" already meant the code around a model. The phrase
*harness engineering* became common in early 2026.

- Phil Schmid (January 2026) described the agent harness as the infrastructure
  that wraps a model to manage long-running tasks, and said it is not the agent
  itself. He extended Karpathy's analogy: model = CPU, context = RAM,
  harness = operating system, agent = application
  ([philschmid.de](https://www.philschmid.de/agent-harness-2026)).
- Mitchell Hashimoto (February 2026) gave the most practical definition:
  whenever an agent makes a mistake, engineer a fix so it never makes that
  mistake again. His fixes were updates to `AGENTS.md` plus small,
  purpose-built scripts
  ([mitchellh.com](https://mitchellh.com/writing/my-ai-adoption-journey)).
- OpenAI published "Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first
  world" (February 2026). It describes a team that designs the environment
  while agents write the code
  ([OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/)). **[Secondary]**:
  the page could not be read for this chapter. Its widely repeated figures
  (code volume, team size, number of pull requests) are therefore not
  reproduced here.
- LangChain summarized the idea as "Agent = Model + Harness"
  ([LangChain, March 2026](https://www.langchain.com/blog/the-anatomy-of-an-agent-harness)).
- Birgitta Böckeler's article on martinfowler.com (April 2026) reframed harness
  engineering for teams that *use* coding agents
  ([martinfowler.com](https://martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/harness-engineering.html)).
- Anthropic documented harness patterns for long-running agents
  ([November 2025](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents);
  [March 2026](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/harness-design-long-running-apps))
  **[Vendor]**.

These definitions emphasize different things. Hashimoto's is incremental,
OpenAI's is organizational, Schmid's and LangChain's are architectural, and
Böckeler's treats the harness as a control system.

## How prompt, context, and harness relate

| Layer | Question it answers | Typical artifacts |
|---|---|---|
| Prompt engineering | How should the instruction be worded? | System prompt, few-shot examples |
| Context engineering | Which tokens should the model see at this step? | Retrieval, tool selection, compaction, memory files, sub-agent summaries |
| Harness engineering | What system makes the model reliable over many steps? | Agent loop, sandbox, hooks, tests and linters, evaluator agents, state logs, permissions |

LangChain calls prompt engineering "a subset of context engineering," and
Anthropic calls context engineering its "natural progression." Treat the chain
*prompt ⊂ context ⊂ harness* as a **teaching heuristic**, not a settled
taxonomy: it appears mostly in explainers, not in primary lab writing.

The more precise statement is that the harness *contains* context management,
but it also includes deterministic machinery, such as linters, sandboxes, and
permission checks. That machinery affects the model only when its output is
fed back into the context.

**Is it just a rebrand?** In part. Retrieval, summarization, and RAG all
predate the label, and some experienced developers dismiss the term as
rebranded prompt engineering
([Addy Osmani](https://addyo.substack.com/p/context-engineering-bringing-engineering)).
What is new is treating these techniques as **one budgeted design problem for
multi-step agents**, which a prompt-only view hides.

## Context engineering

### Right information, right format, right time {#right-info-format-time}

The course's definition splits the work into three questions. Each one names
a different part of the system to inspect.

| Axis | Question to ask | Typical techniques | Closest family below |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Right information** | Did the agent retrieve the most relevant content for this task? | Search tools, agentic search, combining search methods | Select |
| **Right format** | Is what was retrieved clean, structured, and free of duplicates and noise? | Deduplication, pruning, compaction, summaries, structured metadata | Compress |
| **Right time** | Does the content arrive when it is needed, and not before? | Just-in-time retrieval, memory that stores and reloads state | Select and write |

Formatting covers more than headers and layout. A summary is also a format:
it consolidates information so that the important details stand out.

The three axes and the four families of technique (Section
\@ref(four-families)) describe the same work from two angles. Use the axes to
diagnose a problem: *is the issue what was found, how it was presented, or
when it arrived?* Then pick a technique from the families to fix it.
Section \@ref(agentic-search) covers the first axis, right information, in
depth.

### What is in the context window {#context-components}

Before you change anything, list the kinds of context your agent handles. In
a simple chatbot there were only three: the system prompt, the user's input,
and the model's reply. RAG added retrieved documents. An agent adds several
more:

- **System prompt.** The standing instructions. It sits at the front of every
  call, so it should be short and stable. Anything that changes per request
  belongs elsewhere. A stable prefix also keeps the prompt cache warm (Section
  \@ref(context-cost)).
- **User input.** The request, plus any later turns in the conversation.
- **Memory.** Stored information that is reloaded when relevant, such as user
  preferences or task instructions.
- **Reasoning traces.** The agent's own planning and intermediate thinking.
- **Tool context.** Tool definitions, the inputs the model sends, the outputs
  that come back, and any retrieved data.

The course's running example is a ticket-refund agent. A customer asks for a
refund and gives an order number. The agent calls a lookup tool to fetch the
order, calls a policy-search tool to read the refund rules, calls a refund
tool, and replies. Every one of those steps adds tool inputs and outputs to
the context.

**The context only grows, and it is resent in full.** The model is stateless,
so the harness sends the whole accumulated context again on every call. That
includes the system prompt, every tool definition, and every earlier tool
output. Two consequences follow:

- *Growth compounds.* If each turn adds 10% to the context, it roughly doubles
  after seven turns ($1.1^7 \approx 1.95$). If each turn adds 150%, which is
  plausible for a coding agent that reads files and runs tests, a context that
  starts at 1,000 tokens passes one million tokens during the eighth turn
  ($1{,}000 \times 2.5^7 \approx 610{,}000$ and $1{,}000 \times 2.5^8 \approx
  1.5$ million).
- *What people wrote is the smallest part.* In the course's token breakdown for
  a short refund request, the largest categories were the system prompt, the
  tool definitions, and the tool outputs. All three are resent on every call.
  The customer's message, the tool arguments, and the final answer were barely
  visible. The cost you pay is the *sum* of the context sizes over all calls,
  not the size of the final context.

### Context is a finite attention budget

The founding premise is that *more context can make results worse*. Anthropic
describes a finite "attention budget" and names **context rot**: recall falls
as the token count grows. The goal it sets is "the smallest set of high-signal
tokens" that makes the desired outcome likely.

Evidence:

- **Lost in the middle.** Accuracy was highest when the relevant information sat
  at the beginning or end of a long input, and worse in the middle
  ([Liu et al., arXiv 2307.03172](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)).
- **Context rot.** Across 18 models, performance degraded as input length grew,
  often unevenly
  ([Chroma, July 2025](https://www.trychroma.com/research/context-rot)).
  **[Vendor]**: Chroma sells retrieval infrastructure, and the study is not peer
  reviewed.
- **Focused versus full history.** In the same report, Chroma used questions
  from the LongMemEval benchmark
  ([Wu et al., arXiv 2410.10813](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10813)), where
  each question is about one exchange buried in a long chat history. A *full*
  prompt held the whole history (about 113,000 tokens on average). A *focused*
  prompt held only the few relevant messages (about 300 tokens). The answer was
  present in both versions. Every model tested did significantly better on the
  focused prompt. Thinking modes improved both conditions but did not close the
  gap **[Vendor]**.

A practical consequence: a larger advertised context window is a capacity
limit, not a promise that the model will use every token equally well. The
course separates two quantities:

- **Advertised context length**: the maximum number of tokens a model accepts
  in one call.
- **Effective context length**: how much of that the model can use reliably
  for a given task. It depends on the model, the task, and how the content is
  arranged, so there is no universal cut-off.

In the course, Chroma's instructor says the effective length can be as low as
20% to 40% of the advertised length. That figure does not appear in the
context rot report itself **[Unverified]**. Treat it as an order of
magnitude, and measure on your own task.

**Context rot is a size problem; the failures below are quality problems.**
Rot comes from how attention behaves as the window fills, and it happens even
when every token is correct. The four failure modes in the next section come
from what the content says, and they can occur in a context of a few hundred
tokens. A long history makes quality failures more likely, because there are
more chances for two pieces to contradict each other, but the two problems
need different fixes.

### Four ways context fails {#four-failures}

Breunig's taxonomy pairs each failure with a fix
([How long contexts fail](https://www.dbreunig.com/2025/06/22/how-contexts-fail-and-how-to-fix-them.html)).
The examples he cites are secondhand and were not checked against the
original papers for this chapter.

| Failure | What happens | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| **Poisoning** | A hallucination or error enters context and is reused as if true | Validate before writing to memory; prune; quarantine |
| **Distraction** | A long history crowds out the task; the agent repeats past actions | Summarize or compact; start fresh with a handoff note |
| **Confusion** | Irrelevant tools or documents degrade choices | Load fewer tools; retrieve selectively |
| **Clash** | New information contradicts earlier context | Remove stale content; keep one source of truth |

**One conversation, four failures.** The course shows how all four can occur
in a single short refund conversation. The company has just extended its
refund window from 15 to 45 days, but both policy files are still in the
document store.

| Step in the conversation | Failure | Why it happened |
|---|---|---|
| The policy search returns the old 15-day file, and the agent denies a valid refund | **Poisoning** | Outdated content entered the context, and nothing marked it as outdated |
| The customer pushes back; a second search returns the 45-day file, and both versions now sit in context | **Clash** | Two plausible rules conflict, and neither says which one is in force |
| The customer says "just cancel it"; the agent calls the cancellation tool instead of the refund tool | **Confusion** | The two tool descriptions overlap, so an imprecise word picks the wrong action |
| A side question triggers a web search that returns a long page of raw HTML | **Distraction** | Irrelevant content, some of it sharing keywords like "refund", crowds out the task |

The customer ends up with no tickets and no money. None of these were failures
of the model's reasoning. Each came from what the harness let into the context.

The course uses the same four names with slightly broader meanings than
Breunig's:

- Its *poisoning* includes stale retrieved documents, not only hallucinations
  that get reused.
- Its *confusion* is about options too similar to tell apart. Those can be
  overlapping tool descriptions, or three products that share a name.
  Breunig's version is about superfluous tools or documents.
- Its *distraction* is irrelevant content crowding the task, not only a long
  history.

The fixes are the same either way.

**Evidence in the context is not enough.** In the course's first lab, a small
local model (Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B) received the whole knowledge base on every
query. It still sided with a marketing draft over the binding pricing policy,
even though the policy carried an effective date and the draft carried a note
saying the policy had not been updated. A frontier model would often resolve
that conflict. But companies sometimes run small models on their own
infrastructure to keep customer data private, and a production system should
not rely on the model making the right inference. Remove the stale or
conflicting content before it reaches the model, as Section
\@ref(tools-and-hooks) shows.

### Four families of technique: write, select, compress, isolate {#four-families}

LangChain groups the techniques into four families
([LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/blog/context-engineering-for-agents)).

1. **Write: persist state outside the window.** Scratchpads, progress notes, and
   to-do files let an agent recover after its history is trimmed. Manus has the
   agent rewrite a `todo.md` so its goals stay at the *end* of the context, a
   direct counter to lost-in-the-middle.
2. **Select: retrieve just in time.** Keep lightweight identifiers (file paths,
   table names, saved queries) and load content only when needed. Claude Code
   combines an up-front `CLAUDE.md` with on-demand file search. Selection
   applies to tools too: a smaller, relevant toolset reduces confusion.
3. **Compress: summarize or prune.** Compaction replaces old history with a
   summary that keeps decisions, open issues, and key details, and drops
   redundant tool output.
4. **Isolate: give sub-tasks clean windows.** A sub-agent explores in its own
   context and returns a short summary (Anthropic suggests roughly 1,000 to
   2,000 tokens). Isolation costs extra tokens, and some practitioners argue
   that splitting work across agents fragments shared understanding. Choose it
   for parallel, separable work, not by default.

Supporting guidance from the
[Anthropic guide](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents):

- Write system prompts at the "right altitude": specific enough to guide
  behavior, but heuristic rather than a brittle list of rules (Section
  \@ref(system-prompt-altitude) compares the three levels).
- Use a few diverse, canonical examples rather than every edge case.
- Make tools self-contained, robust to errors, and clearly distinct from one
  another. Return compact tool outputs, not raw dumps.

### Right information: agentic search {#agentic-search}

Select is the family that decides *what* reaches the window. The course's
second module treats it through **agentic search**: the agent, not the
developer, decides what to look for, where, and how, and it can search again
after reading the first results.

The contrast is with a fixed retrieval pipeline. Classic RAG (Section
\@ref(retrieval-augmented-generation-rag)) runs the same steps on every
request:

| Decision | Fixed pipeline (basic RAG) | Agentic search |
|:---------|:---------------------------|:---------------|
| What to look for | The user's query, perhaps rewritten once | The agent breaks the task into its own sub-queries |
| Where to look | One index, chosen by the developer | Any source it has a tool for: documents, code, logs, a database |
| How to match | One retriever, usually vector search | The search method that suits each sub-query |
| When to stop | After one retrieval step | When the evidence is enough, or an iteration limit is hit |
| Recovery from a bad first result | Only if the developer built a fallback | The agent refines the query and searches again |

The course's example: support staff notice that similar tickets are not
escalated consistently, and an engineer asks a coding agent to investigate. The
agent searches the code for the escalation logic, finds several factors
(category, an order ID, internal rules), searches further for each, and then
writes SQL to find two tickets with the same category and urgency but
different escalation outcomes. The pair shows the cause: tickets without an
order ID were never escalated. No single search would have found it.

A marketing analog: "why does the brand-lift dashboard disagree with the
vendor's study?" may need the metric definition (documents), the transformation
code (code search), last night's pipeline warnings (logs), and the exposed and
control counts (SQL).

Agentic search has three costs:

- **Less predictable.** The same request can take different paths on
  different runs, which makes testing harder.
- **Slower and more expensive.** Each search is another model call, and the
  whole context is resent each time (Section \@ref(context-components)).
- **More context.** Every tool result is appended, so a thorough search fills
  the window fast. Compress and isolate are the counterweights.

#### Which search method fits the question {#search-methods}

The course frames the choice the way a person would: *what am I looking for,
where does it live, and how should I match it?*

| What you are looking for | Method | Marketing example |
|:-------------------------|:-------|:------------------|
| An exact name, ID, or error code | Exact lexical match, or a regex for a pattern | `campaign_id = 'Q3-BRAND-07'`; every `_dedupe_` helper |
| Several terms, some more important than others | Ranked lexical search (BM25: rare terms and frequent matches score higher) | "frequency cap weekly CTV" |
| An idea that may be worded differently | Semantic search over embeddings | "how do we avoid counting a household twice?" |
| An idea *and* an exact term | Hybrid search: run both, then fuse the rankings | "how is frequency capped, and where is `MAX_FREQ_PER_WEEK` set?" |
| Current records, counts, statuses | A read-only SQL tool (retrieval, not search) | spend by campaign last week |
| What actually happened at run time | Regex over log files | warnings in last night's pipeline run |

Two details matter in practice:

- **Tokenization decides what lexical search can find.** If an identifier
  such as `MAX_FREQ_PER_WEEK` is indexed as one token, a search for
  `frequency` will not match it. Code often needs preprocessing before
  lexical search works well.
- **Semantic search is weak on exact strings.** Embeddings capture meaning,
  so an error code, ticket ID, or file name may rank below a chunk that
  merely talks about the same topic.

**Hybrid search and reciprocal rank fusion.** Semantic and BM25 scores live on
different scales, so adding them is meaningless. Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF)
combines **ranks** instead [@cormack2009rrf]:

$$\text{RRF}(d) = \sum_{r \in R} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)}$$

Each ranked list $r$ contributes more for documents near its top. A document
found by both methods collects two contributions and rises. The constant
$k = 60$ comes from the original paper and flattens the curve, so the top
rank of one list does not dominate. The weights $w_r$ are a common extension.
The original formula has none.

```python
def weighted_rrf(rankings: dict[str, list[str]], weights: dict[str, float],
                 k: int = 60) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    """Fuse ranked lists by rank, not score. Ranks start at 1."""
    scores: dict[str, float] = {}
    for method, ranked_docs in rankings.items():
        for rank, doc in enumerate(ranked_docs, start=1):
            scores[doc] = scores.get(doc, 0.0) + weights[method] / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)


# "How is frequency capped, and where is MAX_FREQ_PER_WEEK set?"
semantic = ["reach_guide.md", "pacing.md", "budget_faq.md", "glossary.md",
            "dsp_notes.md", "audience.md", "brand_lift.md", "frequency.py"]
lexical = ["frequency.py", "config.yaml"]

for w_sem in (1.0, 3.0):
    fused = weighted_rrf({"semantic": semantic, "lexical": lexical},
                         {"semantic": w_sem, "lexical": 1.0})
    order = [doc for doc, _ in fused]
    print(f"weights {w_sem:.0f}:1 -> top: {order[0]}, "
          f"config.yaml at position {order.index('config.yaml') + 1} of {len(order)}")
# weights 1:1 -> top: frequency.py, config.yaml at position 4 of 9
# weights 3:1 -> top: frequency.py, config.yaml at position 9 of 9
```

`frequency.py` ranks only eighth semantically but first lexically, so fusion
puts it on top. The second line shows a trap the course lab points out. With
$k = 60$, rank 1 scores only about 30% more than rank 20 ($1/61$ against
$1/80$), so a 3:1 weight outweighs any rank difference. `config.yaml`, found
only by the keyword search, drops to last: **a lopsided weight does not reduce
a method's influence, it removes it.** Start with equal weights.

#### Tool descriptions decide which search runs

The agent never sees how a tool works. It sees the name, the description, and
the input schema (Section \@ref(designing-tools-a-model-can-use-well)). For
search tools, the course suggests a description should answer three questions
for the model:

1. **Should I call this tool?** Name the data source and the matching method:
   "metric definitions and methodology docs, matched by meaning."
2. **How should I call it?** Say what a good input looks like: "a natural-
   language description of the concept, not a list of keywords" for semantic
   search; "the exact identifier, spelled in full" for lexical search.
3. **What will I get back?** Describe the result: "up to `n` chunks of about
   1,000 characters, each with file path and line number."

Two more parts settle close calls. **When not to use it**, and **its
limits**: a semantic tool returns relevant matches, not all matches, so it
cannot prove that something is absent. Where tools overlap, **name the
alternative**: "for an exact column name, use `symbol_lookup` instead."

The danger phrase is "best for general exploration." It describes almost any
request, so the model may choose that tool for everything.

#### Tool registries: load definitions on demand {#tool-registries}

Detailed descriptions have a price. Tool definitions behave like part of the
system prompt: they are sent on every call, whether or not the tool is used.
In a diagram by Drew Breunig shown in the course, OpenAI's Codex coding
agent already holds about 5,500 tokens before the user types anything, and
roughly a quarter of that is tool definitions (as shown in the course, not
independently checked). A log-search step does not need the definition of a
PDF-export tool.

A **tool registry** keeps most definitions out of the window:

1. Store every tool's name and description in a searchable index, usually a
   vector store.
2. Give the agent one always-loaded tool: `search_tools(query)`.
3. When the agent needs a capability, it searches, and the matching
   definitions are added to the context. Only then can it call those tools.

The course reports that the lab's registry cut token use by more than 40%
(as described in the course, not reproduced here). It can also reduce context
confusion, because fewer look-alike tools compete for each choice.

The costs are real:

- **One more component.** An embedding model, an index, and a search step,
  all of which can fail.
- **A missed tool is invisible.** If the right tool is not in the top $k$
  results, the agent never knows it existed. Measure how often the right tool
  is retrieved, as Appendix \@ref(context-labs-m2) does.
- **Interaction with caching (author's judgment).** Definitions appended
  after the cached prefix keep the cache warm. Rewriting the tool list at the
  top of the request invalidates it (Section \@ref(context-cost)). Check how
  your framework inserts loaded tools.

The course lab's rule of thumb: consider a registry with more than about ten
tools, when most tools are rarely used, or when definitions reach 10,000
tokens or more. With a handful of tools that are used on most tasks, load them
all. Anthropic now ships this as a platform feature, the
[tool search tool](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool):
tools marked `defer_loading` stay out of the context until a regex or BM25
search finds them. Its documentation gives similar thresholds **[Vendor]**.

#### Where agentic search fails {#search-failures}

Start where Section \@ref(look-at-traces) left off: read traces and find
answers that a knowledgeable colleague would have got right. Then locate the
failure. The course's two examples cover both ends: an agent that answered
from code when a policy document stated the rule directly, and an agent that
insisted a database field did not exist because the class definition had been
split across two chunks.

| Where it failed | What the trace shows | Usual fix |
|:----------------|:---------------------|:----------|
| Wrong tool | A lexical search where meaning mattered, or the reverse | Expand descriptions; disambiguate overlapping tools; add a usage example |
| Right tool, wrong source | The search ran over code when the answer was in the docs | State each tool's data source plainly |
| Right tool, bad arguments | Missing parameters, keywords where a sentence was expected | Describe the input format; give an example call |
| Right call, wrong data | The relevant chunk was missing, split, or ranked too low | Data preparation: chunking, metadata, more results, better ranking |

Before fixing anything, turn the failures into a small eval:

- **Collect reference searches.** Include the failures you found *and*
  searches that already work, so you can catch regressions.
- **Change one thing at a time.** Then you know what caused the change in
  the score.
- **Grade at the right level.** Grade the tool input when one call is
  clearly correct. Grade the tool output or the final answer when several
  paths are equally good.

Chapter \@ref(evaluating-agentic-systems) covers component-level evals in
general. Here, tool-selection accuracy is the component metric.

#### Data preparation is context engineering {#data-preparation}

When the right tool runs with the right query and still returns the wrong
chunks, the problem is in how the data was prepared. This looks like data
engineering, but it decides what can ever reach the window.

- **Chunk size and overlap.** Embedding models accept limited input, so long
  text is split. A little overlap between neighboring chunks keeps a sentence
  cut at a boundary readable. Too much overlap fills the top results with
  repeats.
- **Split on structure, not on character count.** Recursive splitting tries
  paragraph breaks first, then lines, then sentences, then words. Markdown
  can be split at its headings, keeping each section whole.
- **Parse code.** A parser turns code into an abstract syntax tree (AST), so
  chunks follow functions and classes instead of cutting a class in half. A
  class split across two chunks caused the course's "missing field" error.
- **Attach metadata.** Store the file path, line numbers, symbol name, and
  document date with each chunk. Metadata lets the agent find a chunk's
  neighbors. It also allows **filtering before ranking**, such as "only
  current methodology docs" or "only this client", which shrinks the
  candidate set. Section \@ref(metadata-context) makes the same argument for
  analytics tables.
- **Enrich small chunks.** Prepend a short summary of the surrounding
  section or file so the chunk carries its context with it.

Measure each change with **precision@k** (of the $k$ chunks retrieved, the
share that is relevant) and **recall@k** (of the relevant chunks, the share
retrieved). This requires a small ground-truth set: for each representative
question, the chunks a correct answer needs.

```python
def precision_recall_at_k(retrieved: list[str], relevant: set[str], k: int):
    """Precision@k and recall@k for one query."""
    hits = len(set(retrieved[:k]) & relevant)
    return hits / k, hits / len(relevant)


# Ground truth for "how do we compute incremental reach?": 4 chunks
relevant = {"reach.md#2", "reach.md#3", "dedup.sql#1", "glossary.md#7"}
retrieved = ["reach.md#2", "faq.md#1", "reach.md#3", "pacing.md#4",
             "glossary.md#7", "reach.md#1", "budget.md#2", "faq.md#3"]
p, r = precision_recall_at_k(retrieved, relevant, k=8)
print(f"precision@8 = {p:.2f}, recall@8 = {r:.2f}")
# precision@8 = 0.38, recall@8 = 0.75
```

The missing chunk is `dedup.sql#1`, the code that actually removes duplicate
households. A metadata filter to methodology docs and SQL, or a lexical leg
for "dedup", is the kind of fix to try next.

The levers pull against each other:

| Change | Precision | Recall | Why |
|:-------|:----------|:-------|:----|
| Smaller chunks | Usually up | Can fall | Less irrelevant text per chunk, but neighbors lose their context |
| More overlap | Can fall | Can fall | Repeated text crowds distinct chunks out of the top $k$ |
| Metadata filter | Up | Same or up | Irrelevant candidates are removed before ranking |
| Larger $k$ | Down | Up | More chunks, and more noise in the window |

The course's advice: keep overlap small and let metadata place each chunk in
its context. Chapter \@ref(evaluating-agentic-systems) has a fuller precision
and recall example.

**Evidence: how much chunking matters.** Chroma's 2024 technical report
([Evaluating chunking strategies for retrieval](https://www.trychroma.com/research/evaluating-chunking),
linked from the course) compared chunking methods on five corpora with 472
LLM-generated questions **[Vendor]**. It scored *tokens* rather than whole
chunks: how much of the passage that answers the question was retrieved,
and how much retrieved text was wasted.

- **The choice matters, but not enormously.** Recall differed by up to 9%
  across strategies.
- **A plain default is hard to beat.** A recursive splitter with 200-token
  chunks and no overlap scored well on every metric, though it was not the
  best on any. Chunkers that use embeddings or an LLM to place boundaries won
  individual metrics, at a much higher compute cost.
- **Overlap cuts both ways.** Less overlap improved efficiency, because
  overlap repeats text. But with a small embedding model (the one the course
  labs use), removing overlap lowered recall. Test overlap; do not assume it.
- **Large default chunks did worst.** OpenAI Assistants' default at the
  time, 800-token chunks with 400 overlapping, scored lowest on most metrics.

The authors note their own limits: questions written by an LLM, a small and
narrow dataset, and run time left out (LLM-based chunking took up to tens of
minutes). Treat the results as a reason to measure on your own data, not as
settings to copy.

#### Very large inputs: recursive language models {#recursive-lms}

Some inputs will never fit: a year of ad-server logs, or 800 MB of agent
traces. In the course's second interview, Drew Breunig describes
**recursive language models (RLMs)**, a test-time strategy from
[Zhang and Khattab (2025)](https://alexzhang13.github.io/blog/2025/rlm/):

- The large input is **not** put in the context. It is loaded as a variable
  in a code environment (a REPL, such as a Python notebook).
- The model writes code to inspect it: look at the first few hundred
  characters, detect that it is JSON lines, count, filter, and sample.
- It can **call a sub-model on a slice**, which gets a fresh context window
  and the same code environment. That recursion gives the method its name.
- Only what the model pulls out of the variable enters its context.

Breunig's argument: models are strong at coding and reasoning but weak with
very long contexts, so turn the long-context problem into a coding problem.
In this chapter's terms, an RLM combines select (the model pulls only what it
needs) with isolate (sub-calls get clean windows), using code execution as the
tool (Chapter \@ref(tool-use)).

This is early research. The authors report gains on long-context benchmarks
**[Vendor]** (the authors' own results), and Breunig's enthusiasm is his
opinion. For an analyst, the familiar version is already common practice: do
not paste the 2 GB file into the chat; let the agent query it with code.

### Cost: the overlooked dimension {#context-cost}

Agents read far more tokens than they write. Manus reports a ratio of roughly
100 input tokens per output token and calls the KV-cache hit rate the most
important production metric **[Vendor]**. Cached input tokens are much cheaper
than uncached ones, which leads to rules such as:

- keep the prompt prefix stable (a timestamp at the top breaks the cache);
- append to the context rather than editing earlier turns;
- serialize JSON deterministically; and
- disable tools by masking them rather than removing their definitions.

These rules **conflict** with compaction and dynamic tool removal, which
invalidate the cache. Good designs compress rarely and in large steps rather
than continuously.

Manus also advises leaving failed attempts in context so the model avoids
repeating them, which seems to contradict "poisoning." One reasonable
reconciliation (the author's judgment): *observed* error messages are useful
feedback, while *unverified claims stored as facts* are harmful.

### Context features are becoming platform features

Vendors now ship these techniques as features, for example Anthropic's
[context editing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing),
[memory tool](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool),
[server-side compaction](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction),
[tool search](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool)
(Section \@ref(tool-registries)), and the progressive disclosure built into
Agent Skills
(Chapter \@ref(claude-code-skills)). Learn the four families. The API names
will change, but the families will still apply.

## Harness engineering

### What is in a harness

A short working definition: **the harness is everything except the model
weights.** LangChain's list includes system prompts; tools, skills, and MCP
servers (Chapter \@ref(model-context-protocol)); infrastructure such as a
filesystem, sandbox, or browser; orchestration such as sub-agents and model
routing; and hooks or middleware for deterministic steps
([LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/blog/the-anatomy-of-an-agent-harness)).

It helps to separate:

- the **builder harness**: the product runtime (Claude Code, the Claude Agent
  SDK, Codex, LangChain Deep Agents, a custom agent); and
- the **user harness**: what *your team* adds on top, such as `AGENTS.md`,
  specs, tests, linters, hooks, permissions, and CI.

Most data scientists work mainly on the user harness, or build a small builder
harness inside an application.

### Tools and hooks: the two levers {#tools-and-hooks}

Context-management components enter a harness in one of two forms.

A **tool** is a function the *model* chooses to call. It has four parts:

| Part | What it is | Does the model see it? |
|---|---|---|
| Tool definition | Name, description, and input schema | Yes; it is the only part the model ever reads |
| Tool input | The structured request (usually JSON) the model emits | Yes; the model writes it |
| Tool implementation | The code that runs | No; it stays in the harness |
| Tool output | What the code returns | Only after the harness appends it to the next call |

Tool use can fail in four places. The model may skip a tool it needed, call
the wrong tool, or call the right tool with the wrong arguments. The first
three usually trace back to the tool description, which works like a
docstring and must say clearly when to use the tool. The fourth failure is the
subtle one: the right tool is called with the right argument, but the data
behind it is wrong. In the course example, the policy search did exactly what
was asked and returned an outdated file. No amount of prompt or description
work fixes that, because the model cannot reject content it has no reason to
doubt.

A **hook** is a function the *harness* runs when a specific event happens. The
model never sees it, never requests it, and cannot skip it. Hooks are
deterministic.

- A **pre-tool hook** runs before a tool executes. Examples: check that the
  user is allowed to use the tool, or block a request that was already
  answered.
- A **post-tool hook** runs after the tool returns and before its output
  enters the context. Examples: drop stale documents, deduplicate, truncate, or
  validate a schema.

Where a hook is wired in varies by system. The course labs call post-tool hooks
from inside the tool, which leaves the agent loop untouched. Claude Code fires
`PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` hooks from the harness itself (Chapter
\@ref(claude-code-hooks)). Either way, the model does not know the hook exists.

The sketch below is a post-tool hook for the stale-policy problem, applied to
marketing metric definitions. It assumes every document carries an effective
date. That metadata is the precondition, and it is data-governance work
(Section \@ref(metadata-context)). Without it, no hook can tell old from
current.

```python
from datetime import date


def keep_current_versions(docs: list[dict], today: date) -> list[dict]:
    """Post-tool hook: keep only the version of each document in effect today."""
    current: dict[str, dict] = {}
    for doc in docs:
        if doc["effective"] > today:  # drafts and future versions are not in effect yet
            continue
        best = current.get(doc["name"])
        if best is None or doc["effective"] > best["effective"]:
            current[doc["name"]] = doc
    return list(current.values())


# What a search tool might return for "how do we define reach and lift?"
retrieved = [
    {"name": "reach.md", "effective": date(2024, 1, 1), "text": "Reach = unique households exposed"},
    {"name": "reach.md", "effective": date(2026, 3, 1), "text": "Reach = unique persons exposed"},
    {"name": "lift.md", "effective": date(2025, 6, 1), "text": "Lift = test rate / control rate - 1"},
    {"name": "lift.md", "effective": date(2027, 1, 1), "text": "Lift (draft) = incremental conversions"},
]

for doc in keep_current_versions(retrieved, today=date(2026, 11, 14)):
    print(doc["name"], doc["effective"], "|", doc["text"])
# reach.md 2026-03-01 | Reach = unique persons exposed
# lift.md 2025-06-01 | Lift = test rate / control rate - 1
```

One short function prevents two failures. The retired version cannot poison
the answer, and with only one version in context there is nothing to clash
with. It also saves tokens on every later call, because the dropped documents
are never resent. Nothing else changed: not the prompt, the model, nor the
agent loop. This is the course's main argument for hooks: when a rule can be
written in code, enforce it in the harness rather than hoping the model
infers it.

### Guides and sensors

Böckeler classifies harness controls on two axes
([martinfowler.com](https://martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/harness-engineering.html)):

| | **Computational** (deterministic, cheap, reliable) | **Inferential** (model-based, slower, non-deterministic) |
|---|---|---|
| **Guides** (before the agent acts) | Templates, schemas, scaffolding scripts, type definitions | `AGENTS.md`, specs, feature lists, skills |
| **Sensors** (after the agent acts) | Tests, linters, type checks, schema validation, data-quality checks | AI code review, LLM judges, evaluator agents |

Prefer computational sensors wherever they can answer the question, and use
inferential ones for judgments that code cannot make. Böckeler also notes the
limits: tests do not catch a misdiagnosed problem, over-engineering, or a
misunderstood instruction.

### Each pattern fixes a named failure

| Recurring failure | Harness response | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Declares success too early | Feature list where every item starts "failing"; checklist before exit; stop hooks that require evidence | Anthropic (Nov 2025), LangChain [Vendor] |
| Tries to do everything at once | Work on one feature per session; commit after each | Anthropic (Nov 2025) [Vendor] |
| Edits tests to pass | Explicit rule against changing tests; protected test files; CI | Anthropic (Nov 2025) [Vendor] |
| Loses track over long runs | Progress log, setup script, descriptive commits, handoff notes | Anthropic (Nov 2025) [Vendor] |
| Praises its own mediocre work | A separate evaluator agent that exercises the result | Anthropic (Mar 2026) [Vendor] |
| Repeats the same failing edit | Loop detection that interrupts the agent | LangChain (Feb 2026) [Vendor] |
| Repeats a known mistake | Add a rule to `AGENTS.md` or a deterministic check | Hashimoto (Feb 2026) |

**Documentation is part of the harness, and long documents rot.** Several
practitioners, OpenAI reportedly among them **[Secondary]**, replaced one large
instruction file with a short index that points to focused documents. This is
the same idea as progressive disclosure in skills and just-in-time retrieval.

**Security gaps.** The primary harness posts reviewed say little about
permissions, sandboxing, secret handling, or prompt injection through tool
outputs. Treat these as first-class harness components anyway: apply least
privilege, require human approval for actions that write, spend, or send, and
keep secrets out of context (see Chapters \@ref(claude-code-hooks) and
\@ref(model-context-protocol)).

### The thin-harness debate

Rich Sutton's "Bitter Lesson" argues that general methods that scale with
compute eventually beat hand-built cleverness. Applied to agents, it raises the
question of whether harness logic is a temporary crutch.

- **Thin-harness view.** Anthropic writes that every harness component
  "encodes an assumption about what the model can't do on its own." When a
  stronger model arrived, it removed parts of its own harness
  ([Anthropic, March 2026](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/harness-design-long-running-apps))
  **[Vendor]**. Schmid recommends harnesses that make yesterday's clever logic
  easy to delete.
- **Harness-matters view.** With the model held fixed, LangChain changed only
  its harness and raised its Terminal-Bench 2.0 score from 52.8% to 66.5%
  ([LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/blog/improving-deep-agents-with-harness-engineering))
  **[Vendor]**. A May 2026 position paper argues that harness-induced variance
  can exceed model-induced variance and can reverse model rankings
  ([arXiv 2605.23950](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23950)); it is an argument,
  not a controlled meta-analysis.

The two views are compatible. *Specific* components (elaborate prompts, rigid
step structures, large tool collections) are absorbed as models improve. The
*need* for an environment, verification, persistent state, and permissions
remains.

**Practical implication:** a leaderboard score measures a model–harness pair.
When you compare models for your own application, hold the harness constant,
and when you change the harness, hold the model constant.

### Prompt debt

In a conversation recorded for the course, Drew Breunig described a pattern
he calls **prompt debt**, by analogy with technical debt. This is a
practitioner's opinion, not a measured result.

1. A team under pressure to ship gives a prompt to the largest frontier model
   and lets it work out the path. It succeeds most of the time, and the demo
   looks great.
2. In use, edge cases keep appearing. Each fix is another line in the prompt:
   a special rule, capital letters, a threat or a bribe.
3. Those patches are tuned to one model's quirks. The prompt becomes long,
   brittle, and hard to change, and switching to a new model means starting
   over.

The teams that get out of prompt debt tend to converge on the ideas DSPy is
built around: make AI behave more like software, with contracts. In practice
that means:

- typed inputs and outputs;
- retry logic;
- structured prompts with schemas; and
- breaking one large call that does twenty things into smaller steps, each
  with its own eval.

Breunig also offered a threshold. If an agent is wrong about 10% of the time,
people stop using it, because they must check every result and might as well
do the work themselves. Teams often add a human in the loop to cover the gap,
as coding agents do. But the enterprise value he sees most often comes from
narrow workflows with *no* human in the loop, where the task is small enough
to make reliable.

This connects to the rest of the chapter. Hashimoto's rule, "engineer a fix so
the mistake never recurs", can be followed in two ways. Adding another line to
the prompt builds prompt debt. Adding a deterministic check, hook, or test
does not. The author's judgment is to use the prompt for judgment calls and
put every rule that can be written as code into the harness.

### Look at your traces {#look-at-traces}

A complaint from a user tells you *that* something went wrong, but the user
messages and the agent's replies alone rarely show *why*. To diagnose a
context problem, you need to see what entered the context at each step.

- A **trace** is the full record of one task: user inputs, agent responses,
  every tool call with its input and output, the agent's reasoning, every
  model call, and any housekeeping the harness did, such as compaction.
- A **span** is one step inside the trace, for example a single tool call with
  its input and output.

A trace can hold more than the model saw. A hook's log of which documents it
dropped belongs in the trace, but it was never sent to the model.

Capturing *what* happened is ordinary logging. A logging hook that fires on
each tool call can write to a file or to a tracing platform. The course names
Arize, LangSmith, and Weights & Biases; on Databricks, MLflow Tracing plays
this role.

Capturing *why* is harder, because the reasoning is usually not in the
replies. The course shows two options:

- Ask the model to think step by step inside tags such as `<think>`, and log
  those blocks.
- Add a `reason` field to each tool's input schema. The model then states its
  objective, why it picked this tool, and why it chose these arguments, and
  the reason is logged with the call.

```python
# A tool definition with a reason field; the exact wrapper format varies by vendor.
search_metrics_tool = {
    "name": "search_metric_definitions",
    "description": "Return the governed definition of one or more marketing metrics.",
    "parameters": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "metric_names": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}},
            "reason": {
                "type": "string",
                "description": (
                    "Your current objective, why this tool helps, "
                    "and why you chose these metric names."
                ),
            },
        },
        "required": ["metric_names", "reason"],
    },
}
```

Two cautions, both the author's judgment:

- **The reason field costs tokens on every call.** Its description is part of
  the tool definition, which is resent on every call, and the model's answer
  adds to the tool input. Measure that cost.
- **A stated reason is the model's self-report, not ground truth.** Use it to
  find where to look, and confirm with the actual inputs and outputs.

Reading traces is the input to error analysis (Section
\@ref(agentic-error-analysis)). Once you can name a failure in the traces, you
can build an eval that measures whether a context-engineering fix worked.

### Evaluation is a harness too

Anthropic's guide to agent evaluation distinguishes the *evaluation harness*
from the *agent harness* and defines tasks, trials, graders, transcripts, and
outcomes
([Anthropic, January 2026](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)):

- **Graders** can be code-based (tests, exact match, schema checks), model-based
  (rubrics, pairwise comparison), or human (expert review).
- **Grade outcomes, not paths.** Judge what the agent produced, but keep
  transcripts for debugging and for spotting reward hacking, such as an agent
  editing the tests it is graded on.
- **pass@k versus pass^k.** pass@k is the chance that *at least one* of *k*
  attempts succeeds; pass^k is the chance that *all k* succeed. For a
  production tool that users run repeatedly, pass^k is the more honest
  reliability measure.

For a statistician, this is familiar ground: define the estimand (task
success), use repeated trials to estimate variance, and avoid grading on the
training set (tasks the harness was tuned on). Chapter
\@ref(evaluating-agentic-systems) covers the vendor-neutral method:
end-to-end and component evals, error analysis, and error bars.

## Applying both to Databricks analytics apps

The design principle that follows from the evidence is:

> **The model chooses and explains; governed engines compute; sensors verify.**

This is the author's synthesis rather than an official Databricks rule, but
each part has support in the sources above.

### Metadata is the highest-return context {#metadata-context}

Text-to-SQL research suggests that semantic context often matters more than
which frontier model you pick:

- Adding a 4 KB semantic-layer document raised accuracy on 100 retail questions
  from about 46–51% to about 68–69% across three frontier models, and the
  differences between models were not statistically significant in either
  condition
  ([arXiv 2604.25149](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.25149)). This is a single study
  on one domain.
- On the BIRD benchmark, better column descriptions improved accuracy, although
  ambiguous columns still needed expert input
  ([arXiv 2408.04691](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.04691)).
- Automatically profiled metadata helped one team reach the top of the BIRD
  leaderboard
  ([arXiv 2505.19988](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19988)).

Databricks' own Genie guidance is a context-engineering playbook
([Genie best practices](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/genie/best-practices)):

1. Rely on clear Unity Catalog table and column names and descriptions.
2. Start with a small number of tables (the docs suggest five or fewer).
3. Prefer **SQL expressions** for metrics, filters, and dimensions, then
   **example SQL** for complex questions, and use plain-text instructions only
   as a last resort.

[Unity Catalog metric views](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/uc-semantics/metric-views/)
define each measure once (reach, overlap rate, lift, support, confidence) so
that every app and agent computes it the same way.

For an analytics team, this is good news: the highest-return work is data
governance work you may already own. Column comments, metric definitions, and
verified example queries now have a new consumer.

### Mapping to the three workloads

| Workload | Context engineering | Harness engineering | Evaluation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Streamlit analytical apps** on Databricks Apps | Send aggregates (top-N, group-bys, summary statistics), not audience-level rows. Keep few tables in scope. Keep a stable system-prompt prefix | On-behalf-of-user auth so Unity Catalog row filters and column masks apply per user. The model proposes SQL or tool parameters; tables and charts render from the result DataFrame, not from model text | A code check that every number in the narrative appears in the result table; an LLM judge for groundedness |
| **Reusable jobs** (lookalike, audience overlap, basket analysis) | Unity Catalog comments on seed, segment, and transaction tables; metric views for overlap, lift, support, and confidence; a few verified example queries for tricky logic such as fiscal calendars | Expose validated logic as Unity Catalog functions or job-triggering tools via MCP. For coding agents that maintain the job code, a short `AGENTS.md` map plus tests act as guides and sensors | Compare results with known gold outputs; measure pass^k across repeated runs; protect unit tests from agent edits |
| **AI-assisted apps** on Databricks foundation models (Genie, Agent Bricks, custom agents) | Follow the Genie order of instruction types; retrieve methodology documents just in time with AI Search rather than preloading them | Gateway quotas and budgets; guardrails; durable memory only for state that must persist. Inference logging stores whatever enters context, so keep personal data out | Genie benchmarks; [MLflow GenAI evaluation](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor) with code scorers and judges; labeled cases where the app should ask for clarification or refuse |

Relevant Databricks references:
[Databricks Apps authorization](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/databricks-apps/auth),
[managed MCP servers](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/agents/mcp-tools/managed-mcp)
(Public Preview), and the
[Foundation Model APIs supported models](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/machine-learning/foundation-model-apis/supported-models)
page. Product names change often: Genie spaces are now called Genie Agents,
Vector Search is now AI Search, and AI Gateway is now Unity Gateway. Check each
docs page's preview banner before relying on a feature.

### Three cautions for marketing data

1. **Schema confusion is tool confusion.** Too many tables in scope degrade
   text-to-SQL the same way too many tools degrade tool choice. Curate.
2. **Client data in prompts is both a privacy risk and a cost.** Aggregate
   first, enforce minimum cell sizes, and use per-user authorization.
3. **Do not let the assistant grade its own narrative.** A deterministic check
   against the result table is cheaper and more reliable than asking a model
   whether its lift or overlap summary is correct.

## A minimal sketch: the number-check sensor

This illustrative check implements the third caution. It is an instructional
example, not tested production code, and the regular expression handles only
simple number formats.

```python
import re

import pandas as pd


def numbers_in_text(text: str) -> set[float]:
    """Extract plain numbers such as 12, 3.5, 1,200 or 45% from narrative text."""
    tokens = re.findall(r"-?\d[\d,]*\.?\d*", text)
    return {round(float(t.replace(",", "")), 2) for t in tokens}


def unsupported_numbers(narrative: str, result: pd.DataFrame) -> set[float]:
    """Return numbers in the narrative that do not appear in the result table."""
    numeric = result.select_dtypes("number").to_numpy().ravel()
    allowed = {round(float(x), 2) for x in numeric}
    allowed |= {round(float(x) * 100, 2) for x in numeric}  # shares shown as %
    return numbers_in_text(narrative) - allowed


result = pd.DataFrame({"segment": ["A", "B"], "overlap_rate": [0.18, 0.07]})
narrative = "Segment A overlaps 18% with the seed audience, versus 9% for B."
print(unsupported_numbers(narrative, result))  # {9.0} -> flag for review
```

In a harness, this check runs after the model writes its summary. If it finds
unsupported numbers, the app either asks the model to revise using only the
table or shows the table without the narrative.

**Hands-on.** Appendix \@ref(context-labs) walks through the course labs for
this chapter: triggering the four failure modes, measuring how an agent's
context grows, filtering stale policies with a post-tool hook, giving a coding
agent seven search tools, and loading tool definitions from a registry.

## Exercise: audit one AI-assisted app

Choose an existing assistant or prototype and answer:

1. **Context inventory.** List everything in the context window on a typical
   request, using the components in Section \@ref(context-components). Estimate
   tokens for each, and how much each grows per turn. Remember that everything
   is resent on every call. What could be removed or loaded just in time?
2. **Failure mapping.** Read the full trace of one real failure, not just the
   final answer. Classify it as poisoning, distraction, confusion, or clash,
   or as a harness failure such as premature success or missing verification.
   Then say which axis failed: information, format, or timing.
3. **One guide, one sensor.** Add one guide (a metric definition, example query,
   or `AGENTS.md` rule) and one computational sensor (a schema check, number
   check, or test).
4. **Measure.** Build 20 to 30 representative questions with known answers. Run
   each several times and report pass^k before and after your change, holding
   the model constant.
5. **Search audit.** For five real questions, write down where a careful
   colleague would look and how they would match: an exact ID, keywords, a
   concept, SQL, or logs (Section \@ref(search-methods)). Compare that with the
   tools the agent called in its traces. For one question, list the ground-truth
   chunks and compute precision@k and recall@k.

## Key takeaways

- **Context engineering** decides what the model sees at each step; **harness
  engineering** builds the system that makes many steps reliable.
- Treat *prompt ⊂ context ⊂ harness* as a useful heuristic, not an official
  taxonomy; the harness also includes deterministic parts that never enter the
  context.
- Give the agent the right information, in the right format, at the right
  time. Use these three axes to diagnose a problem, and the four families to
  fix it.
- Context is a finite attention budget: more tokens can reduce quality. Use the
  four families—write, select, compress, isolate—and watch the cost trade-off
  with caching.
- Context rot is a size problem; poisoning, clash, confusion, and distraction
  are quality problems. Effective context length is shorter than the
  advertised length, and the whole context is resent on every call.
- Agentic search lets the agent choose what to search, where, and how, and
  search again. It finds better context at the cost of predictability, time,
  and context size. Match the method to the question: exact match for IDs,
  BM25 for keywords, embeddings for concepts, RRF to fuse both, SQL for
  records.
- When search fails, locate the failure before fixing it: wrong tool, wrong
  source, bad arguments, or the right call returning the wrong chunks. The
  last one is a data-preparation problem; measure it with precision@k and
  recall@k.
- Tool definitions are resent on every call. With many rarely used tools, a
  tool registry loads definitions on demand, at the risk of never retrieving
  the right one.
- The model chooses tools, while the harness runs hooks. When a rule can be
  written as code, enforce it with a hook rather than more prompt text, which
  builds prompt debt.
- Look at traces, not just final answers; they are the input to error
  analysis and evals.
- Organize harness controls as guides and sensors, and prefer deterministic
  sensors where possible. Each harness component should fix a named failure.
- Benchmarks measure a model–harness pair. Hold one fixed when you evaluate the
  other, and report pass^k for reliability.
- On Databricks, governed metadata is the best context, deterministic functions
  and jobs are the best tools, and numbers should come from query results.
- Expect specific techniques and API names to expire; the separation of
  concerns is the durable lesson.
